CI measures line coverage per Go package. A **new** package must reach at least **68%** before its first pull request
can be merged; existing packages must not drop by more than two percentage points in a single pull request.

Coverage is a smoke alarm, not a goal. A test that only executes code without asserting anything is worse than no test,
because it hides the gap.

## Confirming an outage

A single failed check never pages a customer. A monitor is marked **Down** only when the failure is confirmed from
at least two probe locations within the same check cycle. If only one location fails, the monitor goes to **Degraded**
and we re-check from a third location straight away. This removes most false alarms caused by a bad network path near
one location.

Heartbeat monitors work the other way round: there is no probe, and the monitor goes Down when the expected ping does
not arrive within the grace period the customer configured.

## Background

Probe workers run in 11 locations. Each location has its own small Kubernetes cluster (or, for Hetzner and Vultr, a
k3s cluster) that runs the `probe-worker` deployment. Workers pull jobs for their location from the scheduler and
publish results back to the central results stream.

All commands below assume your context points at the right location cluster and namespace:

```bash
nwctl kube use probes --location fra1
kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=beacon-probes
```

# Runbook: Redis Sentinel

Beacon uses Redis for rate limiting, alert de-duplication and short-lived locks. Nothing in Redis is durable: if we lose
it, rate limits reset and a few alerts may be sent twice. That is annoying, not catastrophic.

## Troubleshooting

- **Port already in use**: something else (often an old Postgres from Homebrew) is listening. `lsof -i :5432` shows
  what.
- **Go module download fails**: check that `GOPRIVATE=github.com/northwind/*` is set; bootstrap adds it to your shell
  profile.
- **ClickHouse eats your memory**: lower `max_server_memory_usage` in `dev/clickhouse/config.xml`.

## ClickHouse is the bottleneck

- Check `system.merges` and `system.parts` for tables with thousands of active parts. Too many parts means inserts are too
  small; raise the ingester batch size (`INGEST_BATCH_ROWS`) temporarily.
- Check disk usage on every ClickHouse node. Merges stop when a disk is nearly full.
- Hand over to the Platform team if a ClickHouse node is unhealthy.

## Monitoring

The "Postgres" dashboard shows replication lag, connections per pool, slow queries and disk usage. Alerts fire on
replication lag above 30 seconds, disk usage above 80%, and failed backups.

## Common causes

| Cause | How it looks | What to do |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ClickHouse inserts slow | Insert latency up, ingester CPU low | Check merges and disk on ClickHouse; see below |
| Ingester pods crashing | Restarts in `kubectl get pods`, lag grows in steps | Logs, then roll back the last ingester deploy |
| Burst after a drained location comes back | Lag spikes once, then falls | Usually clears itself; scale up if it does not |
| One noisy account | Results per second jumps for one `account_id` | Throttle the account (below) |

## Hotfixes

A hotfix skips the train. Use it only for customer-visible bugs that cannot wait for the next train, or security fixes.

```bash
git checkout -b hotfix/2026.08.3-hf1 release/2026.08.3
git cherry-pick <sha-from-main>
git push -u origin hotfix/2026.08.3-hf1
```

The fix must land on `main` first (or at the same time), so the next train does not undo it. Hotfixes still need the
normal review and green CI.

## Setup

Each production region runs three Redis nodes (one primary, two replicas) and three Sentinel processes that watch them
and promote a replica when the primary fails. Clients connect to Sentinel first to find out which node is the primary.

| --- | --- | --- |

| Sentinel | 26379 | Same hosts, separate process |

The master group name is `beacon`. Quorum is 2.

## Clusters

We run Postgres ourselves on EC2, managed by Patroni with etcd for leader election. All clusters run
**PostgreSQL 15.6** with the same configuration template; differences are only in instance size and replica count.

| Cluster | Environment | Region | Nodes | Instance type |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `pg-main-euc1` | production | eu-central-1 | 1 primary, 2 replicas | r6i.2xlarge |
| `pg-main-use2` | production | us-east-2 | 1 primary, 2 replicas | r6i.xlarge |
| `pg-staging` | staging | eu-central-1 | 1 primary | m6i.large |

Replicas are in different availability zones from the primary. Patroni fails over automatically when the primary is
unreachable for 30 seconds.

## Postgres

Base backups and WAL archiving are handled by **pgBackRest**, which runs on every Patroni node and pushes to the
`nwl-pg-backups-euc1` and `nwl-pg-backups-use2` buckets. Backups are encrypted with a KMS key per region, and each
bucket has Object Lock so a compromised account cannot delete them.

Because WAL is archived continuously, we can restore to any point in time within the retention window, usually with a
loss of under a minute of data.

## Confirming an outage

A single failed check never pages a customer. A monitor is marked **Down** only when the failure is confirmed from
at least two probe locations within the same check cycle. If only one location fails, the monitor goes to **Degraded**
and we re-check from a third location straight away. This removes most false alarms caused by a bad network path near
one location.

Heartbeat monitors work the other way round: there is no probe, and the monitor goes Down when the expected ping does
not arrive within the grace period the customer configured.

Restores never overwrite a running production cluster. You restore into a new cluster, check it, and then switch
services over (or copy the rows you need).

## Life of a check

1. A customer creates a monitor. `beacon-api` stores it in Postgres.
2. The `scheduler` reads monitor definitions every few seconds and emits a check job for each monitor that is due, one
   job per probe location the monitor is assigned to.
3. A `probe-worker` in that location picks up the job, runs the check (HTTP request, TCP connect, DNS lookup, ...) and
   publishes the result to the `RESULTS` stream on **NATS JetStream**.
4. The `ingester` consumes the stream, writes every raw result to ClickHouse, and keeps the current state of each
   monitor in Postgres.
5. When the state changes, the `ingester` emits an event that the `notifier` turns into alerts according to the
   customer's alert rules.

Jobs and results are small (under 2 KB each). At peak we process about 14,000 results per second across all regions.

## Background

Probe workers publish every result to the `RESULTS` stream. The `ingester` deployment reads it through the durable
consumer `ingester`, writes raw results to ClickHouse in batches, and updates monitor state in Postgres. Alerts are
evaluated after the write, so a backlog delays alerts too. That is why this alert pages.

```bash
make bootstrap
```

When it finishes, `make doctor` checks that everything is in place and prints what is missing.

# Beacon architecture

This page describes how Beacon is put together: the services, how a check travels through the system, where data lives
and which regions we run in. It is meant for new engineers and for anyone writing a design doc. Operational detail
(ports, commands, dashboards) lives in the `ops/` pages.

## Services

| Service | Language | Owner | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `beacon-api` | Go | Core API | Public REST API and the backend of the dashboard |
| `web` | TypeScript (Next.js) | Web | Dashboard and public status pages |
| `scheduler` | Go | Probes | Turns monitor definitions into check jobs on a fixed cadence |
| `probe-worker` | Go | Probes | Runs checks from a probe location and reports results |
| `ingester` | Go | Probes | Stores results and decides whether a monitor changed state |
| `notifier` | Go | Core API | Sends alerts to channels (email, Slack, SMS, webhooks, ...) |
| `billing` | Go | Revenue engineering | Plans, invoices, usage metering, Stripe integration |

All Go services live in the `beacon` monorepo; the web app lives in `beacon-web`. Every service ships as a container
image and runs on Kubernetes (EKS), deployed with Argo CD.

## Background

Probe workers run in 11 locations. Each location has its own small Kubernetes cluster (or, for Hetzner and Vultr, a
k3s cluster) that runs the `probe-worker` deployment. Workers pull jobs for their location from the scheduler and
publish results back to the central results stream.

All commands below assume your context points at the right location cluster and namespace:

```bash
nwctl kube use probes --location fra1
kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=beacon-probes
```

## Versioning

Backend releases use calendar versioning in the form `YYYY.MM.N`, where `N` counts releases within the month and starts
at 1. Example: the third release in August 2026 is `2026.08.3`. Hotfixes add a patch suffix: `2026.08.3-hf1`.

The dashboard (`beacon-web`) deploys continuously and does not carry a version number. The public API is versioned
separately by its URL path; see [API guidelines](api-guidelines.md).

# Production deploys

How a backend release gets to production, how we watch it, and how we roll it back. The weekly rhythm and versioning are
in [Release process](../engineering/release-process.md). Staging works differently; see [Staging](deploy-staging.md).

## The release train

We release the backend once a week on a fixed schedule, so nobody has to ask "when will this be out?".

1. The release branch is cut from `main` every week on **Wednesdays at 11:00 CET** by the release bot. Whatever is merged
   by then is on the train.
2. The branch deploys to staging automatically and soaks there for 24 hours. QA runs the regression suite during the
   afternoon.
3. The release captain promotes the branch to production the next day, following the production deploy steps.
4. The release bot posts the release notes in #releases and on the public changelog.

If the train is cancelled (holidays, a freeze, an open SEV1), the release captain announces it in #releases and the next
train takes everything.

## Toolchain

We pin tool versions with `mise`, which reads the `.tool-versions` file at the root of each repository. After installing
mise, it picks the right versions automatically when you `cd` into a repository.

| Tool | Version | Used for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Go | Go 1.22.5 | All backend services |
| Node.js | Node.js 20.11 (LTS) | `beacon-web` and the docs site |
| pnpm | 9.x | JavaScript packages |
| golangci-lint | 1.59 | Go linting, also run in CI |
| Terraform | 1.8 | Only if you work on `terraform/` |

Please do not install a different Go or Node version globally "just to try". Version drift between laptops and CI is the
most common cause of "works on my machine".

## Database migrations

Migrations run as a pre-sync hook before the new pods start. They must be backwards compatible with the previous
release, because during the canary both versions run at the same time. Destructive changes (dropping a column) happen in
a later release, after the code that used the column is gone. See [Database](database.md).

## Pagination

All list endpoints use cursor pagination. Offsets are not supported, because results change too quickly for offsets to
be stable.

- Request: `?limit=50&cursor=<opaque>`. The default `limit` is 50, the maximum is 200.
- Response: the items are in `data`, and the cursor for the next page is in `next_cursor`. When there are no more
  pages, it is `null`.

```json
{
  "data": [{ "id": "mon_8f2k1", "name": "Checkout API" }],
  "next_cursor": "eyJpZCI6Im1vbl84ZjJrMSJ9"
}
```

## Basics

- JSON in, JSON out. Field names in `snake_case`.
- Base URL: `https://api.getbeacon.io/v2/`. The major version is in the path.
- Authentication with a bearer token: `Authorization: Bearer <token>`. Tokens are created in the dashboard and scoped to
  one workspace.
- Timestamps are RFC 3339 strings in UTC (`2026-08-14T09:30:00Z`).
- IDs are opaque strings with a type prefix: `mon_`, `ale_`, `inc_`, `chn_`.

## Canary

Every service rolls out with Argo Rollouts. The canary takes 10% of traffic first and **bakes for 25 minutes** while
automated analysis compares error rate, latency and check-result volume with the stable version. If any metric is

After the bake, traffic moves to 50% for five minutes and then to 100%.

### Staging

- The staging pooler listens on port 6432 on `pgbouncer.db.svc.cluster.local` in `nw-staging-euc1`.
- It uses session pooling, so you can use prepared statements and advisory locks when debugging.

### Production

- Production PgBouncer listens on port **6543**. The DNS name is `pgbouncer.db.svc.cluster.local` inside the cluster.
- Pool size is 40 server connections per database per PgBouncer pod, with three pods per region.
- Prepared statements are disabled in the services' drivers because of transaction pooling.

## Nightly reset

Staging data is not precious. Every night at **03:15 UTC** a job drops the staging Postgres and ClickHouse databases and
reseeds them from the fixtures in `dev/fixtures/`. The reset takes about ten minutes; the API returns `503` while it
runs.

If you are testing something that must survive a night, create it again in the morning or ask in #beacon-platform to
skip one reset.

## Troubleshooting

- **Port already in use**: something else (often an old Postgres from Homebrew) is listening. `lsof -i :5432` shows
  what.
- **Go module download fails**: check that `GOPRIVATE=github.com/northwind/*` is set; bootstrap adds it to your shell
  profile.
- **ClickHouse eats your memory**: lower `max_server_memory_usage` in `dev/clickhouse/config.xml`.

## Clusters

We run Postgres ourselves on EC2, managed by Patroni with etcd for leader election. All clusters run
**PostgreSQL 15.6** with the same configuration template; differences are only in instance size and replica count.

| Cluster | Environment | Region | Nodes | Instance type |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `pg-main-euc1` | production | eu-central-1 | 1 primary, 2 replicas | r6i.2xlarge |
| `pg-main-use2` | production | us-east-2 | 1 primary, 2 replicas | r6i.xlarge |
| `pg-staging` | staging | eu-central-1 | 1 primary | m6i.large |

Replicas are in different availability zones from the primary. Patroni fails over automatically when the primary is
unreachable for 30 seconds.

## Connecting

Services never connect to Postgres directly. They go through PgBouncer, which runs as a sidecar-free deployment in each
cluster in transaction pooling mode.

## Restoring Postgres

Restores never overwrite a running production cluster. You restore into a new cluster, check it, and then switch
services over (or copy the rows you need).

1. Open an incident or a change ticket, and say what point in time you need.
2. Create a restore cluster from the backup:

   ```bash
   nwctl backups restore --env prod --region euc1 --target-time "2026-08-14 09:30:00+00" --into pg-restore-1
   ```

3. Verify the data on the restore cluster with a read-only shell.
4. Either copy the rows you need back with a reviewed script, or fail over the services to the restore cluster
   following the Patroni runbook.
5. Delete the restore cluster when you are done; it costs real money.

A hotfix skips the train. Use it only for customer-visible bugs that cannot wait for the next train, or security fixes.

```bash
git checkout -b hotfix/2026.08.3-hf1 release/2026.08.3
```

## Feature flags and releases

Big features ship dark behind a flag and are enabled separately from the release (see [Feature flags](feature-flags.md)).
That way the release train never waits for a feature to be "ready".

## Rolling out

1. Merge with the flag off everywhere.
2. Turn it on in staging and for the internal Northwind workspace.
3. Turn it on for a few friendly customers (a segment in the flag tool), then by percentage.
4. At 100% for a week without trouble, open the cleanup pull request.

Rolling back is turning the flag off. Make sure the "off" path still works after the "on" path has been live for a
while; for instance, data written by the new path must still be readable by the old one.

| Raw check results (one row per check run per location) | 400 days | Partition dropped in ClickHouse |
| Hourly and daily aggregates (uptime %, response times) | 25 months | Deleted |
| Incidents and alert history | 3 years | Deleted |
| Monitor definitions and alert rules | While the account exists | Deleted with the account |
| Status page subscribers (email addresses) | Until they unsubscribe | Deleted within 7 days |
| Webhook payloads we sent | 30 days | Deleted |

The dashboard shows less history than we store, depending on the plan (see [Pricing](../product/pricing.md)). Upgrading
makes older history visible again, as long as it is still within the period above.

## Stack

| Piece | What we use | Where |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Metrics | Prometheus, one per cluster | In-cluster, 15 days of raw samples |
| Long-term metrics | Thanos (sidecar, store, compactor) | S3 bucket per region |

## Capacity

Each worker handles about 400 concurrent checks. The horizontal pod autoscaler scales on queue time, between 4 and 40
pods per location. If a location is pinned at its maximum, raise it in `deploy/probes/<location>/values.yaml` and tell
the Probes team.

## Postgres

Base backups and WAL archiving are handled by **pgBackRest**, which runs on every Patroni node and pushes to the
`nwl-pg-backups-euc1` and `nwl-pg-backups-use2` buckets. Backups are encrypted with a KMS key per region, and each
bucket has Object Lock so a compromised account cannot delete them.

Because WAL is archived continuously, we can restore to any point in time within the retention window, usually with a
loss of under a minute of data.

## What is backed up

| Data | Method | Frequency | Retention |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Postgres (all production clusters) | Base backup plus continuous WAL archiving | Nightly base backup at 01:00 UTC | 35 days |
| ClickHouse raw results | `clickhouse-backup` to S3 | Weekly full, daily incremental | 8 weeks |
| S3 buckets (exports, status page assets) | Versioning and cross-region replication | Continuous | 90 days for old versions |
| Redis | Not backed up | | Rebuilt from Postgres if lost |
| Staging | Not backed up | | Reset nightly anyway |

## Background

Probe workers run in 11 locations. Each location has its own small Kubernetes cluster (or, for Hetzner and Vultr, a

All commands below assume your context points at the right location cluster and namespace:

## The release train

We release the backend once a week on a fixed schedule, so nobody has to ask "when will this be out?".

1. The release branch is cut from `main` every week on **Wednesdays at 11:00 CET** by the release bot. Whatever is merged
   by then is on the train.
2. The branch deploys to staging automatically and soaks there for 24 hours. QA runs the regression suite during the
   afternoon.
3. The release captain promotes the branch to production the next day, following the production deploy steps.
4. The release bot posts the release notes in #releases and on the public changelog.

If the train is cancelled (holidays, a freeze, an open SEV1), the release captain announces it in #releases and the next
train takes everything.

## Release captain

The captain rotates weekly among backend engineers; the schedule is pinned in #releases. The captain:

- watches the staging soak and decides whether to promote,
- follows up on regressions found by QA,
- writes the customer-facing summary for the changelog,

## How deploys work

Staging deploys itself. Every merge to `main` builds new images, and Argo CD syncs the `deploy/staging/` folder of
`beacon-deploy` within about five minutes. The weekly release branch replaces `main` on staging during its soak, then
staging goes back to following `main`.

- No approvals, no deploy windows, no canary.
- Deploys can happen at any time, including weekends.
- If you need staging to stay on a specific version (for a demo, or to reproduce a bug), pin it:

  ```bash
  ./scripts/pin-staging.sh beacon-api 2026.08.2
  ./scripts/pin-staging.sh --clear beacon-api
  ```

  Pins expire after 48 hours so nobody forgets one.

## Steps

1. Check #incidents. Do not deploy during an open SEV1 or SEV2 unless the deploy is the fix.
2. Run the promotion script from the release branch:

   ```bash
   ./scripts/promote.sh release/2026.08.3 --env prod
   ```

   It opens a pull request in `beacon-deploy` with the new image tags for both regions.
3. Get one approval from another engineer with the `prod-deployer` role, then merge.
4. Argo CD starts the canary in Frankfurt. Watch the "Release health" dashboard and #deploys.
5. When Frankfurt is fully rolled out and healthy, Argo CD continues with Ohio automatically.
6. Post "done" in the release thread in #deploys.

## Rolling out

1. Merge with the flag off everywhere.
2. Turn it on in staging and for the internal Northwind workspace.
3. Turn it on for a few friendly customers (a segment in the flag tool), then by percentage.
4. At 100% for a week without trouble, open the cleanup pull request.

Rolling back is turning the flag off. Make sure the "off" path still works after the "on" path has been live for a
while; for instance, data written by the new path must still be readable by the old one.

## Rate limits

Each API token may make up to **600 requests per minute**. Every response carries `X-RateLimit-Limit`,
`X-RateLimit-Remaining` and `X-RateLimit-Reset`. Over the limit, the API returns `429` with a `Retry-After` header.
Enterprise customers can ask for a higher limit through their account manager.

## Basics

- JSON in, JSON out. Field names in `snake_case`.
- Base URL: `https://api.getbeacon.io/v2/`. The major version is in the path.
- Authentication with a bearer token: `Authorization: Bearer <token>`. Tokens are created in the dashboard and scoped to
  one workspace.
- Timestamps are RFC 3339 strings in UTC (`2026-08-14T09:30:00Z`).
- IDs are opaque strings with a type prefix: `mon_`, `ale_`, `inc_`, `chn_`.

## Scale the ingester

The ingester scales on lag automatically, but the autoscaler is conservative. During a backlog you can scale by hand:

```bash
kubectl -n ingest scale deploy/ingester --replicas=16
```

The hard cap is **24 replicas**. Above that, ClickHouse receives more parallel inserts than it can merge, and the backlog
gets worse, not better. If 24 is not enough, the problem is ClickHouse, not the ingester.

## Common causes

| Cause | How it looks | What to do |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ClickHouse inserts slow | Insert latency up, ingester CPU low | Check merges and disk on ClickHouse; see below |
| Ingester pods crashing | Restarts in `kubectl get pods`, lag grows in steps | Logs, then roll back the last ingester deploy |
| Burst after a drained location comes back | Lag spikes once, then falls | Usually clears itself; scale up if it does not |
| One noisy account | Results per second jumps for one `account_id` | Throttle the account (below) |

## Writing alerts

Alert rules live next to the service in `deploy/alerts/<service>.yaml`. Every rule needs:

- a `severity` label (`page`, `warn` or `info`),
- a `runbook_url` annotation that points to a page in `ops/runbooks/`,
- a `summary` that a tired person can understand at 3 a.m.

Alert on symptoms customers feel (checks late, alerts not sent) rather than on causes (CPU high). Cause-based alerts are
fine as `warn`.

## Alert routing

| Severity | Goes to | When |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `page` | PagerDuty: the rotation that is on shift | Any time |
| `warn` | Slack `#beacon-alerts-low` | Working hours; nobody is woken up |
| `info` | Nowhere; visible in Grafana and Alertmanager only | |

Alertmanager groups alerts by service and region, and waits 30 seconds before sending the first notification of a group
so that one problem produces one page.

## Severity levels

| Level | Meaning | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| SEV1 | Beacon's core promise is broken for many customers | Checks not running in a region; alerts not delivered |
| SEV2 | A major feature is broken or badly degraded | Status pages down; results delayed by more than 10 minutes |
| SEV3 | A minor feature is broken, or a risk with no customer impact yet | One probe location down; backup failing |

# Continuous integration

Every push to a pull request in `beacon` and `beacon-web` runs our CI pipeline on **Buildkite**. This page explains what
the pipeline does, how to read it, and what to do when it is red.

## Pipeline

The pipeline is defined in `.buildkite/pipeline.yml`. Steps run in parallel where they can.

| Step | What it checks | Required |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `lint` | golangci-lint, the custom analyzers, ESLint for the web app | Yes |
| `unit` | Unit tests with coverage per package | Yes |
| `integration` | Integration tests against containers | Yes |
| `openapi` | The OpenAPI file matches the handlers | Yes |
| `build` | Builds every service image and pushes it to ECR with the commit SHA as tag | Yes |
| `e2e-smoke` | A five-minute subset of the Playwright suite against a preview environment | No |

A pull request can be merged only when every required step is green. See [Testing](testing.md) for what the tests
cover and how the coverage gate works.

## Draft pull requests

Open a draft early when you want feedback on the approach. Reviewers do not need to look at drafts unless you ask them
to. Mark the pull request ready when it passes CI and you would be happy to merge it.

## Coverage

CI measures line coverage per Go package. A **new** package must reach at least **68%** before its first pull request
can be merged; existing packages must not drop by more than two percentage points in a single pull request.

Coverage is a smoke alarm, not a goal. A test that only executes code without asserting anything is worse than no test,
because it hides the gap.

## The layers

| Layer | Tooling | Runs | Typical time |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Unit | `go test`, Vitest | On every push | Under 3 minutes |
| Integration | `go test -tags integration` with Testcontainers | On every pull request | About 9 minutes |
| End-to-end | Playwright against staging | After every staging deploy, and nightly | About 20 minutes |
| Load | k6 | Before releases that touch the hot path | On demand |

## Confirming an outage

A single failed check never pages a customer. A monitor is marked **Down** only when the failure is confirmed from
at least two probe locations within the same check cycle. If only one location fails, the monitor goes to **Degraded**
and we re-check from a third location straight away. This removes most false alarms caused by a bad network path near
one location.

Heartbeat monitors work the other way round: there is no probe, and the monitor goes Down when the expected ping does
not arrive within the grace period the customer configured.

## Background

Probe workers run in 11 locations. Each location has its own small Kubernetes cluster (or, for Hetzner and Vultr, a
k3s cluster) that runs the `probe-worker` deployment. Workers pull jobs for their location from the scheduler and
publish results back to the central results stream.

All commands below assume your context points at the right location cluster and namespace:

```bash
nwctl kube use probes --location fra1
kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=beacon-probes
```

# Runbook: Redis Sentinel

Beacon uses Redis for rate limiting, alert de-duplication and short-lived locks. Nothing in Redis is durable: if we lose
it, rate limits reset and a few alerts may be sent twice. That is annoying, not catastrophic.

### Staging

- The staging pooler listens on port 6432 on `pgbouncer.db.svc.cluster.local` in `nw-staging-euc1`.
- It uses session pooling, so you can use prepared statements and advisory locks when debugging.

## Troubleshooting

- **Port already in use**: something else (often an old Postgres from Homebrew) is listening. `lsof -i :5432` shows
  what.
- **Go module download fails**: check that `GOPRIVATE=github.com/northwind/*` is set; bootstrap adds it to your shell
  profile.
- **ClickHouse eats your memory**: lower `max_server_memory_usage` in `dev/clickhouse/config.xml`.

## ClickHouse is the bottleneck

- Check `system.merges` and `system.parts` for tables with thousands of active parts. Too many parts means inserts are too
  small; raise the ingester batch size (`INGEST_BATCH_ROWS`) temporarily.
- Check disk usage on every ClickHouse node. Merges stop when a disk is nearly full.
- Hand over to the Platform team if a ClickHouse node is unhealthy.

## Monitoring

The "Postgres" dashboard shows replication lag, connections per pool, slow queries and disk usage. Alerts fire on
replication lag above 30 seconds, disk usage above 80%, and failed backups.

## ClickHouse

ClickHouse backups exist so that we can rebuild after losing a whole shard. Restoring a single customer's results is not
supported; results are not critical enough to justify it.

## Common causes

| Cause | How it looks | What to do |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ClickHouse inserts slow | Insert latency up, ingester CPU low | Check merges and disk on ClickHouse; see below |
| Ingester pods crashing | Restarts in `kubectl get pods`, lag grows in steps | Logs, then roll back the last ingester deploy |
| Burst after a drained location comes back | Lag spikes once, then falls | Usually clears itself; scale up if it does not |
| One noisy account | Results per second jumps for one `account_id` | Throttle the account (below) |

| High | 7.0–8.9 | 14 days |
| Medium | 4.0–6.9 | 60 days |
| Low | 0.1–3.9 | Next planned upgrade, at most 180 days |

The clock starts when the finding is confirmed, not when the scanner first reports it. Security confirms new findings
within one working day.

## Exceptions

If a fix cannot ship within the SLA (the upstream patch does not exist yet, or the upgrade breaks something), the owning
team asks for an exception:

1. Describe the finding, why it cannot be fixed in time, and what reduces the risk in the meantime.
2. Security approves or rejects within two working days.
3. Exceptions expire after 30 days and must be renewed with fresh reasoning.

## Hotfixes

A hotfix skips the train. Use it only for customer-visible bugs that cannot wait for the next train, or security fixes.

```bash
git checkout -b hotfix/2026.08.3-hf1 release/2026.08.3
git cherry-pick <sha-from-main>
git push -u origin hotfix/2026.08.3-hf1
```

The fix must land on `main` first (or at the same time), so the next train does not undo it. Hotfixes still need the
normal review and green CI.

## Size

Keep pull requests small. The soft limit is **400 changed lines**, not counting generated code, fixtures and lock files.
Larger changes are fine when they are mechanical (a rename, a dependency bump); say so in the description. Otherwise,
split them: a refactor first, the behaviour change second.

## Rolling out

1. Merge with the flag off everywhere.
2. Turn it on in staging and for the internal Northwind workspace.
3. Turn it on for a few friendly customers (a segment in the flag tool), then by percentage.
4. At 100% for a week without trouble, open the cleanup pull request.

Rolling back is turning the flag off. Make sure the "off" path still works after the "on" path has been live for a
while; for instance, data written by the new path must still be readable by the old one.

## Setup

Each production region runs three Redis nodes (one primary, two replicas) and three Sentinel processes that watch them
and promote a replica when the primary fails. Clients connect to Sentinel first to find out which node is the primary.

| Component | Port | Hosts |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Redis | 6379 | `redis-{1,2,3}.cache.euc1.nwl.internal` |
| Sentinel | 26379 | Same hosts, separate process |

The master group name is `beacon`. Quorum is 2.

## Clusters

We run Postgres ourselves on EC2, managed by Patroni with etcd for leader election. All clusters run
**PostgreSQL 15.6** with the same configuration template; differences are only in instance size and replica count.

| Cluster | Environment | Region | Nodes | Instance type |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `pg-main-euc1` | production | eu-central-1 | 1 primary, 2 replicas | r6i.2xlarge |
| `pg-main-use2` | production | us-east-2 | 1 primary, 2 replicas | r6i.xlarge |
| `pg-staging` | staging | eu-central-1 | 1 primary | m6i.large |

Replicas are in different availability zones from the primary. Patroni fails over automatically when the primary is
unreachable for 30 seconds.

## Postgres

Base backups and WAL archiving are handled by **pgBackRest**, which runs on every Patroni node and pushes to the
`nwl-pg-backups-euc1` and `nwl-pg-backups-use2` buckets. Backups are encrypted with a KMS key per region, and each
bucket has Object Lock so a compromised account cannot delete them.

Because WAL is archived continuously, we can restore to any point in time within the retention window, usually with a
loss of under a minute of data.

## Confirming an outage

A single failed check never pages a customer. A monitor is marked **Down** only when the failure is confirmed from
at least two probe locations within the same check cycle. If only one location fails, the monitor goes to **Degraded**
and we re-check from a third location straight away. This removes most false alarms caused by a bad network path near
one location.

Heartbeat monitors work the other way round: there is no probe, and the monitor goes Down when the expected ping does
not arrive within the grace period the customer configured.

Each production region runs three Redis nodes (one primary, two replicas) and three Sentinel processes that watch them and promote a replica if the primary fails. Clients query Sentinel first to discover the primary. Redis listens on port 6379 at hosts redis-{1,2,3}.cache.euc1.nwl.internal; Sentinel uses port 26379 on the same hosts. The master group name is 'beacon' and the Sentinel quorum is 2.

From ops/runbooks/redis-sentinel.md ('Redis Sentinel' — Checking health): run `redis-cli -h redis-1.cache.euc1.nwl.internal -p 26379 sentinel get-master-addr-by-name beacon` and `redis-cli -h redis-1.cache.euc1.nwl.internal -p 26379 sentinel replicas beacon`. All three Sentinels should agree on the primary; if they do not, one Sentinel is partitioned and should be restarted.
The runbook advises that after a full region restart operators must start the Redis nodes before starting the Sentinel processes; if Sentinels start first they will elect no master.

The ops/runbooks/redis-sentinel.md notes Beacon uses Redis for rate limiting, alert de-duplication, and short-lived locks; nothing in Redis is durable, so if Redis is lost rate limits will reset and a few alerts may be sent twice — annoying but not catastrophic.
Beacon uses Redis for rate limiting, alert de-duplication, and short-lived locks; the Redis deployment uses Sentinel and is not considered durable storage.

User's vulnerability management policy sets remediation SLAs: Critical (CVSS 9.0–10.0) — fix deployed to production within 72 hours; High (CVSS 7.0–8.9) — within 14 days; Medium (CVSS 4.0–6.9) — within 60 days; Low (CVSS 0.1–3.9) — next planned upgrade, at most 180 days. t1.text: Staging Postgres is fronted by a pooler listening on port 6432 at pgbouncer.db.svc.cluster.local in the nw-staging-euc1 Kubernetes cluster.
In production, PgBouncer for Postgres listens on port 6543 and is reachable inside the cluster at the DNS name pgbouncer.db.svc.cluster.local.
Services in Beacon never connect to Postgres directly; they connect through PgBouncer, which is deployed sidecar-free in each cluster and configured to use transaction pooling mode.
Services' Postgres drivers have prepared statements disabled in production because transaction pooling (used by PgBouncer) is incompatible with prepared statements.
In local development, Postgres is exposed on port 5432 and provides the 'beacon_dev' database with user 'beacon' and password 'beacon' when started from dev/compose.yaml.
Staging environments are not backed up and are reset nightly.

User's ops/deploy-staging.md states QA runs the regression suite against staging every day between 13:00 and 15:00 CET; engineers must avoid pinning or restarting services during that window because it makes the results useless.
After the release branch is cut it deploys to staging automatically and soaks there for 24 hours; QA runs the regression suite during the afternoon of that soak period.

User's ops/deploy-staging.md states staging is where every change runs before reaching customers; staging is deliberately 'boring' — a single cluster that uses synthetic customers and whose data is thrown away every night. Production deploys are documented in deploy-production.md.
All production Postgres clusters are backed up using base backups plus continuous WAL archiving; a nightly base backup runs at 01:00 UTC and Postgres backups are retained for 35 days.

To check Results backlog in prod-euc1, run: `nwctl kube use prod --region euc1` then `nats --context prod-euc1 consumer info RESULTS ingester` and inspect the 'Unprocessed Messages' and 'Ack Pending' fields; the Results pipeline dashboard shows these numbers over time alongside ClickHouse insert latency.

Each production region runs three Redis nodes (one primary, two replicas) and three Sentinel processes that watch them and promote a replica if the primary fails. Clients query Sentinel first to discover the primary. Redis listens on port 6379 at hosts redis-{1,2,3}.cache.euc1.nwl.internal; Sentinel uses port 26379 on the same hosts. The master group name is 'beacon' and the Sentinel quorum is 2.

From ops/runbooks/redis-sentinel.md ('Redis Sentinel' — Checking health): run `redis-cli -h redis-1.cache.euc1.nwl.internal -p 26379 sentinel get-master-addr-by-name beacon` and `redis-cli -h redis-1.cache.euc1.nwl.internal -p 26379 sentinel replicas beacon`. All three Sentinels should agree on the primary; if they do not, one Sentinel is partitioned and should be restarted.
The runbook advises that after a full region restart operators must start the Redis nodes before starting the Sentinel processes; if Sentinels start first they will elect no master.

The ops/runbooks/redis-sentinel.md notes Beacon uses Redis for rate limiting, alert de-duplication, and short-lived locks; nothing in Redis is durable, so if Redis is lost rate limits will reset and a few alerts may be sent twice — annoying but not catastrophic.
Beacon uses Redis for rate limiting, alert de-duplication, and short-lived locks; the Redis deployment uses Sentinel and is not considered durable storage.

From ops/runbooks/queue-backlog.md (observed 2026-10-10): during a backlog, check disk usage on every ClickHouse node because merges stop when a disk is nearly full, which can make ClickHouse the bottleneck.
ClickHouse raw results are backed up to S3 using the `clickhouse-backup` tool with a weekly full backup and daily incremental backups; ClickHouse backups are retained for 8 weeks.
Beacon uses ClickHouse to store raw check results and aggregates; ClickHouse tables are partitioned by month and retention is governed via the security/data-retention.md policy.

User's vulnerability management policy sets remediation SLAs: Critical (CVSS 9.0–10.0) — fix deployed to production within 72 hours; High (CVSS 7.0–8.9) — within 14 days; Medium (CVSS 4.0–6.9) — within 60 days; Low (CVSS 0.1–3.9) — next planned upgrade, at most 180 days. The remediation clock starts when a finding is confirmed (not when first reported), and Security confirms new findings within one working day.

t0.text: Staging Postgres is fronted by a pooler listening on port 6432 at pgbouncer.db.svc.cluster.local in the nw-staging-euc1 Kubernetes cluster.
In production, PgBouncer for Postgres listens on port 6543 and is reachable inside the cluster at the DNS name pgbouncer.db.svc.cluster.local.
Services in Beacon never connect to Postgres directly; they connect through PgBouncer, which is deployed sidecar-free in each cluster and configured to use transaction pooling mode.
Services' Postgres drivers have prepared statements disabled in production because transaction pooling (used by PgBouncer) is incompatible with prepared statements.
In local development, Postgres is exposed on port 5432 and provides the 'beacon_dev' database with user 'beacon' and password 'beacon' when started from dev/compose.yaml.
Staging environments are not backed up and are reset nightly.

User's ops/deploy-staging.md states QA runs the regression suite against staging every day between 13:00 and 15:00 CET; engineers must avoid pinning or restarting services during that window because it makes the results useless.
After the release branch is cut it deploys to staging automatically and soaks there for 24 hours; QA runs the regression suite during the afternoon of that soak period.

User's ops/deploy-staging.md states staging is where every change runs before reaching customers; staging is deliberately 'boring' — a single cluster that uses synthetic customers and whose data is thrown away every night. Production deploys are documented in deploy-production.md.
All production Postgres clusters are backed up using base backups plus continuous WAL archiving; a nightly base backup runs at 01:00 UTC and Postgres backups are retained for 35 days.

User noted in ops/runbooks/queue-backlog.md (observed 2026-10-10) that probe workers publish every result to the RESULTS stream; the ingester deployment reads it via the durable consumer 'ingester', writes raw results to ClickHouse in batches, and updates monitor state in Postgres. Alerts are evaluated after the write, so a backlog delays alerts and triggers this alert.

To check Results backlog in prod-euc1, run: `nwctl kube use prod --region euc1` then `nats --context prod-euc1 consumer info RESULTS ingester` and inspect the 'Unprocessed Messages' and 'Ack Pending' fields; the Results pipeline dashboard shows these numbers over time alongside ClickHouse insert latency.

Each production region runs three Redis nodes (one primary, two replicas) and three Sentinel processes that watch them and promote a replica if the primary fails. Clients query Sentinel first to discover the primary. Redis listens on port 6379 at hosts redis-{1,2,3}.cache.euc1.nwl.internal; Sentinel uses port 26379 on the same hosts. The master group name is 'beacon' and the Sentinel quorum is 2.

From ops/runbooks/redis-sentinel.md ('Redis Sentinel' — Checking health): run `redis-cli -h redis-1.cache.euc1.nwl.internal -p 26379 sentinel get-master-addr-by-name beacon` and `redis-cli -h redis-1.cache.euc1.nwl.internal -p 26379 sentinel replicas beacon`. All three Sentinels should agree on the primary; if they do not, one Sentinel is partitioned and should be restarted.
The runbook advises that after a full region restart operators must start the Redis nodes before starting the Sentinel processes; if Sentinels start first they will elect no master.

The ops/runbooks/redis-sentinel.md notes Beacon uses Redis for rate limiting, alert de-duplication, and short-lived locks; nothing in Redis is durable, so if Redis is lost rate limits will reset and a few alerts may be sent twice — annoying but not catastrophic.

User's vulnerability management policy sets remediation SLAs: Critical (CVSS 9.0–10.0) — fix deployed to production within 72 hours; High (CVSS 7.0–8.9) — within 14 days; Medium (CVSS 4.0–6.9) — within 60 days; Low (CVSS 0.1–3.9) — next planned upgrade, at most 180 days. The remediation clock starts when a finding is confirmed (not when first reported), and Security confirms new findings within one working day.

The release process requires the hotfix to land on main first (or at the same time) so the next train does not undo it, and hotfixes still require the normal review process and green CI before merging.

User's engineering/testing.md gives the owning team 10 working days to fix or delete a flaky test; if unresolved after that period the issue is escalated to the team lead during the weekly engineering sync.

When a vulnerability fix cannot be shipped within the SLA (for example, because an upstream patch does not exist yet or an upgrade breaks functionality), the owning engineering team must request an exception from Security.
User's engineering/release-process.md states a hotfix skips the train and should be used only for customer-visible bugs that cannot wait for the next train, or for security fixes.

t1.text: For production Postgres connections, PgBouncer listens on port 6543 and is reachable inside the cluster at the DNS name pgbouncer.db.svc.cluster.local.
User's ops/database.md states services never connect to Postgres directly; they route through PgBouncer, which is deployed sidecar-free in each cluster and uses transaction pooling mode.

User's ops/database.md notes the staging PgBouncer pooler listens on port 5433 at pgbouncer.db.svc.cluster.local in the nw-staging-euc1 cluster; it was moved there when staging received its own PgBouncer pods during the Postgres upgrade.

User's engineering/local-dev.md troubleshooting note (2026-10-10): for "Port already in use" errors, an old Postgres from Homebrew often listens on port 5432; run lsof -i :5432 to see which process is using the port.
Services' database drivers have prepared statements disabled in production because PgBouncer uses transaction pooling, which is incompatible with prepared statements.

User's ops/deploy-staging.md states staging databases are reset every night at 03:15 UTC: a job drops the staging Postgres and ClickHouse databases and reseeds them from the fixtures in dev/fixtures/.
The nightly staging reset takes about ten minutes, and while it runs the API returns HTTP 503.
QA runs the regression suite against staging every day between 13:00 and 15:00 CET; engineers must avoid pinning or restarting services during that window because it makes the QA results useless.

User's ops/deploy-staging.md says the staging environment runs on a single cluster, uses synthetic customers, and that all staging data is thrown away every night; production deploys are documented in deploy-production.md.
ops/deploy-staging.md advises that if you are testing something that must survive a night, recreate it in the morning or ask in Slack channel #beacon-platform to skip a single reset.

EU on-call shifts change on Tuesdays at 10:00 CET with a 15-minute handover call between the outgoing and incoming primary; the handover must cover open incidents and follow-ups, alerts that fired more than twice that week (and why), and scheduled work (migrations, provider maintenance, major customer launches). A summary must be written in the handover thread so the US rotation can read it too.

ops/oncall-us.md states that shift chatter goes in #beacon-oncall-us and that at 07:00 CET the US primary posts a short note for the EU primary summarizing what happened overnight and which incidents remain open.

For SEV1 and SEV2 incidents the incident commander must page the secondary on-call engineer and the team that owns the affected service.
The 'ingester' service is written in Go, owned by the Probes team, and stores check results and decides whether a monitor changed state.
A probe-worker in the assigned location picks up the job, executes the check (examples: HTTP request, TCP connect, DNS lookup), and publishes the check result to the RESULTS stream on NATS JetStream.
The 'probe-worker' service is written in Go, owned by the Probes team, and runs checks from a probe location then reports the results.
The ingester consumes the RESULTS stream, writes every raw result to ClickHouse, and maintains the current state of each monitor in Postgres.

The runbook instructs you to inspect the 'Unprocessed Messages' and 'Ack Pending' fields when viewing the RESULTS consumer info; the Results pipeline dashboard graphs these same metrics over time alongside ClickHouse insert latency.

engineering/code-review.md: Keep pull requests small with a soft limit of 400 changed lines (do not count generated code, fixtures, or lock files). Larger changes are allowed when mechanical (e.g., renames, dependency bumps) if stated in the description; otherwise split into a refactor first and the behavior change second.
engineering/code-review.md requires every pull request to have at least one approval from someone other than the PR author before it can be merged.

engineering/code-review.md advises opening a draft pull request early when you want feedback on the approach; reviewers don't need to look at drafts unless you specifically ask them. Mark the pull request ready when it passes CI and you would be happy to merge it.
engineering/code-review.md enforces squash-merge only; the pull request title becomes the resulting commit message, so authors should make PR titles meaningful.

engineering/code-review.md advises that a good pull request description answers three questions: (1) what changes, in one or two sentences; (2) why now, with a link to the Linear issue; and (3) how to verify, describing what was tested and what the reviewer should check first. Include screenshots or a short recording for anything visible in the dashboard.
User's local development doc instructs to clone the Beacon monorepo using: git clone git@github.com:northwind/beacon.git, then cd beacon and run make bootstrap to perform the initial local setup.
The make bootstrap target installs the developer toolchain through mise, fetches Go modules, installs the repository's git hooks, and starts the local dependencies required to run Beacon locally.
All Go services for Beacon live in the 'beacon' monorepo.
ops/deploy-staging.md advises that if you are testing something that must survive a night, recreate it in the morning or ask in Slack channel #beacon-platform to skip a single reset.
User runs the beacon-api locally with the command `make run SERVICE=beacon-api`, which starts the API at http://localhost:8080.

As of 2026-10-10, backend releases use calendar versioning in the form YYYY.MM.N where N counts releases within the month starting at 1 (example: the third release in August 2026 is 2026.08.3). Hotfixes append a patch suffix like 2026.08.3-hf1.
The backend uses a weekly release train: a release branch is cut from main every week on Tuesdays at 14:30 CET by the release bot, and whatever is merged by that cut is included on the train.

The ops/deploy-production.md document describes how a backend release is promoted to production, how the release is monitored (watching), and the documented procedures for rolling back a release if needed.
ops/deploy-production.md points engineers to engineering/release-process.md for the weekly release rhythm and versioning details used when promoting releases to production.
As of 2026-10-10, the beacon-web dashboard deploys continuously and does not carry a version number.

engineering/api-guidelines.md requires all list endpoints to use cursor pagination (offsets are not supported). Requests use ?limit=50&cursor=<opaque> with a default limit of 50 and a maximum of 200. Responses include items in the "data" array and the next page cursor in "next_cursor" (null when no more pages).
From engineering/api-guidelines.md: the API resource 'Results' is at /v2/monitors/{id}/results, is read-only, and returns newest-first results.
As of 2026-10-10, the public API is versioned separately by its URL path; see engineering/api-guidelines.md for details on API versioning.
User's API guideline: Beacon API accepts JSON requests and returns JSON responses; all field names must use snake_case.

As of 2026-10-10, an open question before GA for private probe locations is how long Beacon should retain results from private locations, with some customers wanting results stored only in their own region.

Northwind full-time employees receive 27 days of paid vacation per calendar year, in addition to public holidays; part-time employees receive the same entitlement pro rata (example: someone working four days per week gets 21.6 days, rounded up to 22).
Employees may carry over up to five unused vacation days to the next year, and any carried-over days expire on March 31 of the following year.

Employees are required to take at least one block of two consecutive weeks of vacation each year to ensure rest and reduce single-person dependency (the handbook advises 'your brain needs it, and so does the bus factor').
The company's time-off policy allows up to four days per year to care for a sick family member; if more time is needed, the employee and manager will find a solution together.
User must request vacation days in the HR system Personio at least two weeks before any vacation longer than three days, per handbook/time-off.md (Vacation > Requesting vacation).

As of 2026-10-10, ops/eu-data-residency.md states the EU residency cluster is much smaller than the main data plane but carries a fixed cost of about €6,000 per month before the first customer; contracts include a surcharge to cover this and Sales holds the detailed numbers.

The EU residency cluster has its own Prometheus and Alertmanager; its metrics are not shipped to the shared Thanos bucket, and dashboards for the EU residency cluster read directly from the regional Prometheus.
User's ops/eu-data-residency.md states customers are placed on the EU residency cluster by Sales and Platform together; placement is not self-serve.

If a vulnerability fix cannot ship within the SLA (for example, the upstream patch does not exist yet or an upgrade would break something), the owning team must request an exception that describes the finding, why it cannot be fixed in time, and what reduces the risk meanwhile.

User's vulnerability management remediation SLAs require fixes deployed to production within: Critical (CVSS 9.0–10.0) — 72 hours; High (CVSS 7.0–8.9) — 14 days; Medium (CVSS 4.0–6.9) — 60 days; Low (CVSS 0.1–3.9) — next planned upgrade, at most 180 days.
The owning team has 10 working days from issue creation to fix or delete the flaky test; if unresolved after that period, escalate the issue to the team lead in the weekly engineering sync.

engineering/code-review.md instructs reviewers to pick up review requests within one working day, and to respond within two hours for hotfixes; if they cannot, they should say so and suggest someone else to review.
Security will approve or reject vulnerability-fix exception requests within two working days.

Northwind Labs' handbook (welcome.md) defines 'Deep Work Thursday' on Thursdays: internal meetings (stand-ups, one-on-ones, planning, demos) must not be scheduled; only customer calls, interviews, and incidents are allowed. Employees should block the day in their calendar so the scheduling assistant does not offer it to others.
The Travel policy advises employees to check the team calendar before booking travel to avoid a whole team being away during the same week.
ops/oncall-eu.md instructs engineers to ignore non-paging alerts outside working hours — such alerts should wait until the next morning.
Northwind Labs asks all employees to be reachable between 14:00 and 17:00 CET on working days; US colleagues start earlier so those three hours create overlap with Europe.

If the User is in an on-call rotation, they must swap their on-call shifts before taking vacation and consult the on-call pages in ops/ for details, per handbook/time-off.md (Vacation > Requesting vacation).

The handbook expenses page (handbook/expenses.md, Allowances > Per diem on business trips) says employees traveling for work receive a flat per diem of €48 per travel day for food and small costs with no receipts required; when the company pays for lunch and dinner the allowance is halved and must be claimed in the expenses app with the trip dates.

Northwind's 'Business travel' policy (handbook/policies/travel.md) states travel is occasional — the yearly offsite, some customer visits, and a few conferences — and explains how to book and what the company pays for; spending while away (cards, receipts, daily allowance) is covered in the Expenses page (handbook/expenses.md).
handbook/expenses.md (Expenses > Allowances > Phone) states that employees in an on-call rotation receive €30 per month toward their phone plan and should claim it once per quarter.

User's handbook equipment page (handbook/equipment.md) states the company does not provide phones. On-call employees receive partial reimbursement of their phone plan (see expenses.md) and must install PagerDuty on their own phone. Allowed work apps on personal phones: Slack, Google apps, PagerDuty, and 1Password.

handbook/expenses.md states new joiners receive a one-time home office setup budget of €750 to buy a desk, chair, monitor, and headset; employees must keep receipts and the furniture becomes theirs after two years. The company also pays up to €25 per month toward the employee's internet connection.
The owning team has 10 working days from issue creation to fix or delete the flaky test; if unresolved after that period, escalate the issue to the team lead in the weekly engineering sync.
The testing policy forbids "fixing" a flaky test by adding sleeps; engineers must find and fix the underlying race condition instead.

User's engineering/architecture.md (Beacon architecture: Confirming an outage) states that a single failed check never pages a customer: a monitor is marked Down only when the failure is confirmed from at least two probe locations within the same check cycle. If only one location fails, the monitor is marked Degraded and the system re-checks from a third location immediately.
Vulnerability-fix exceptions expire after 30 days and must be renewed with fresh reasoning when continued unfixability persists.
engineering/testing.md defines a flaky test as one that fails and then passes on retry without any code change.

handbook/onboarding.md: Every new joiner is paired with a buddy from another team for questions they might not ask their manager; the pairing lasts for the first six weeks with at least one half-hour meeting per week. Buddies receive a small budget for a coffee or lunch and claim it as a team expense.
handbook/onboarding.md says new joiners are assigned an onboarding buddy and will meet that buddy during their first week at the company.
Under Northwind's parental leave policy, an employee's onboarding buddy from their onboarding days or their manager will help them catch up on what changed while they were on leave.

handbook/onboarding.md (Onboarding > First month) states the first-month plan: Week 1 — set up accounts and laptop and complete your first merged change or first support shift; Week 2 — understand how Beacon runs a check end-to-end (see engineering/architecture.md); Week 3 — own a small piece of work from start to finish; Week 4 — thirty-day check-in with your manager and People Ops.

handbook/onboarding.md states engineers join the company's on-call rotation only after three months of employment (never earlier). Before an engineer's first on-call shift they must shadow two shifts and participate in a game day run with the Platform team.

Between 19:00 and 07:00 CET, anyone at Northwind (support, sales, or an engineer up late in Europe) who notices production is broken should not try to find a person in Slack but must trigger an incident on the PagerDuty service 'beacon-after-hours'; that service pages the US primary and automatically opens an incident Slack channel.

Support guidance for Status pages (noted 2026-10-10): if a status page shows 'Down' but the user's site is actually up, support should check which monitors are linked to the affected component and inspect those monitors' check history to diagnose false Down states.

If something is broken for many customers, that counts as an incident; the user should notify the on-call engineer via PagerDuty (see the ops/ on-call pages) and post immediately in the #incidents Slack channel rather than waiting for more tickets.
User's ops/oncall-us.md states US on-call engineers must acknowledge pages within the escalation window and be at a laptop shortly afterward.

User's ops/oncall-us.md escalation policy: a page goes to the US primary first; if the primary does not acknowledge within 12 minutes PagerDuty escalates to the US secondary; if neither acknowledges after a further 12 minutes PagerDuty calls the Head of Platform. The window is longer than in Europe because US shifts include late evenings, when it can take a moment to get to a laptop.

User's security/data-retention.md states sales records for customers who never bought are retained for 2 years after the last contact.
As of 2026-10-10, an open question before GA for private probe locations is whether agents should auto-update or remain pinned/managed by the customer.
User's security/data-retention.md specifies audit logs of staff access to production are retained for 2 years.

product/pricing.md states any other discount requests must follow the discount approval rules in the Sales playbook (../sales/playbook.md).

The handbook expenses page states anything purchased for a customer (for example, gifts or dinners) must be approved by the sales lead or the CEO before purchase.

product/pricing.md states that decisions about grandfathering customers for price changes are made jointly by the CEO and the Head of Product.

User's projects require Go version 1.23.2 for all backend services according to the repository's pinned toolchain.

Northwind's parental leave policy states that medical appointments during pregnancy are paid time and do not need to be taken as leave.
